claim: A fairly continuous Laminin-rich BM surrounds the brain from 17 to 18 hpf.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Torres-Paz and Whitlock, 2014; Torres-Paz et al., 2021), we first noticed the appearance of a fairly continuous (with only tiny interruptions) Laminin-rich BM surrounding the brain from 17 to 18 hpf, while around the OP, only discrete Laminin spots were detected at this stage (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and A', and cited previous studies.

claim: Around the OP at 17-18 hpf, only discrete Laminin spots are detected.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Torres-Paz and Whitlock, 2014; Torres-Paz et al., 2021), we first noticed the appearance of a fairly continuous (with only tiny interruptions) Laminin-rich BM surrounding the brain from 17 to 18 hpf, while around the OP, only discrete Laminin spots were detected at this stage (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and A'.

claim: By 22 hpf, two distinct BMs are visible, one around the brain and the other partially enveloping the OP on its basal side.
source: By contrast, at the end of coalescence (22 hpf), two distinct BMs were clearly visible, one around the brain and the other one partially enveloping the OP on its basal side (Figure 1B and B'), suggesting that the Laminin-rich BM of the OP starts to assemble between 18 and 22 hpf, during the late phase of OP coalescence.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B and B'.

claim: The Laminin-rich BM of the OP starts to assemble between 18 and 22 hpf, during the late phase of OP coalescence.
source: By contrast, at the end of coalescence (22 hpf), two distinct BMs were clearly visible, one around the brain and the other one partially enveloping the OP on its basal side (Figure 1B and B'), suggesting that the Laminin-rich BM of the OP starts to assemble between 18 and 22 hpf, during the late phase of OP coalescence.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that discrete spots are present at 18 hpf and a continuous BM is present at 22 hpf.

claim: Mesenchymal cells exhibiting cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP migrate anteriorly around the OP from 17 hpf.
source: From 17 hpf, mesenchymal cells exhibiting cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP were seen to migrate anteriorly around the OP (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Mesenchymal cells exhibiting cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP could represent neural crest cells and/or mesodermally derived cells of the periocular mesenchyme.
source: According to the literature, these cells could represent neural crest cells (NCC; Bryan et al., 2020; Harden et al., 2012; Torres-Paz and Whitlock, 2014) and/or mesodermally derived cells of the periocular mesenchyme (Vöcking et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A subset of RFP+ OP cells display cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP.
source: A subset of RFP+ OP cells also displayed cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP (Figure 1E–H' and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1E-H' and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Laminin γ1 around the OP starts to be deposited mostly during late coalescence stages from at least a subset of OP cells and surrounding mesenchymal cells.
source: Altogether, these live imaging experiments suggest that Laminin γ1 around the OP starts to be deposited mostly during late coalescence stages, from at least a subset of OP cells and surrounding mesenchymal cells.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP in OP cells and mesenchymal cells.

claim: Telencephalic cells exhibit cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP expression throughout OP coalescence.
source: Telencephalic cells also exhibited cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP expression throughout OP coalescence (Figure 1—video 2), suggesting that the forebrain contributes to the deposition of its own Laminin γ1-containing BM at these stages.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—video 2.

claim: The forebrain contributes to the deposition of its own Laminin γ1-containing BM during OP coalescence.
source: Telencephalic cells also exhibited cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP expression throughout OP coalescence (Figure 1—video 2), suggesting that the forebrain contributes to the deposition of its own Laminin γ1-containing BM at these stages.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP in telencephalic cells.

claim: A strong, continuous BM-like signal envelops the brain and the OP at 28 and 36 hpf, except where the olfactory axons leave the OP and enter the brain and above the neuronal rosette where the nostril orifice opens.
source: Using both approaches, we observed a strong, continuous BM-like signal enveloping the brain and the OP at these stages, except (i) where the olfactory axons leave the OP and enter the brain (defined respectively as the exit and entry points, see below) and, as we previously reported (Baraban et al., 2023), (ii) above the neuronal rosette assembling in the dorso-lateral OP, where the nostril orifice opens in the skin (Figure 1C–D' and F–J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 1C-D' and F-J, and cited previous study.

claim: Local disruptions in the BMs ensheathing the OP and the brain occur precisely where the YFP+ axons exit the OP and enter the brain.
source: Immunostaining for Laminin revealed local disruptions in the BMs ensheathing the OP and the brain, precisely where the YFP+ axons exit the OP (exit point) and enter the brain (entry point) (Figure 1C–D').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C-D'.

claim: Small interruptions of the BM are present near the RFP+ axon tips along the ventro-medial wall of the OP by the end of coalescence.
source: By the end of the coalescence, when the BM starts to assemble around the OP, we noticed that small interruptions of the BM were already present near the RFP+ axon tips, along the ventro-medial wall of the OP (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—video 2.

claim: The exit point does not open through local perforation of a pre-existing BM around the OP but through incomplete BM synthesis/assembly in this area.
source: This suggests that the exit point does not open through local perforation of a pre-existing BM around the OP but through incomplete BM synthesis/assembly in this area.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BM interruptions are present as the BM assembles.

claim: The entry point is slightly more dorsal than the exit point (about 10-20 µm).
source: The entry point was slightly more dorsal than the exit point (of about 10–20 µm), and the initial dorsal growth of the RFP+ axons thus occurred between the two BMs (Figure 1F–H').
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1F-H'.

claim: The initial dorsal growth of the RFP+ axons occurs between the two BMs.
source: The entry point was slightly more dorsal than the exit point (of about 10–20 µm), and the initial dorsal growth of the RFP+ axons thus occurred between the two BMs (Figure 1F–H').
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1F-H'.

claim: The opening of the entry point through the brain BM is concomitant with the arrival of the RFP+ axons.
source: The opening of the entry point through the brain BM was concomitant with the arrival of the RFP+ axons, suggesting that the axons degrade or displace BM components to enter the brain (Figure 1G–H' and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1G-H' and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: The axons degrade or displace BM components to enter the brain.
source: The opening of the entry point through the brain BM was concomitant with the arrival of the RFP+ axons, suggesting that the axons degrade or displace BM components to enter the brain (Figure 1G–H' and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the entry point opens when axons arrive.

claim: The entry points often appear as regions with several small BM interruptions rather than as a unique hole in the BM.
source: Note that, as for the exit points, the entry points often appeared as regions with several, small BM interruptions, rather than as a unique hole in the BM (Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1—video 4.

claim: Once in the brain, the distal tip of the RFP+ axons migrates in close proximity with the brain's BM.
source: Once in the brain, as observed in fixed embryos, the distal tip of the RFP+ axons (but not the axon shaft) migrated in close proximity with the brain's BM (Figure 1HI, Figure 1—videos 2 and 4).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1H-I and Figure 1—videos 2 and 4.

claim: The axons first grow dorsally for a short distance between the BMs of the OP and the brain, then their distal tips migrate along the internal side of the brain's BM.
source: Overall our observations indicate that the axons first grow dorsally for a short distance between the BMs of the OP and the brain, then their distal tips migrate along the internal side of the brain's BM (Figure 1K).
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of axon behavior shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The Laminin-rich BMs serve as a migratory path for the axons during their journey from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
source: We thus hypothesise that the Laminin-rich BMs serve as a migratory path for the axons during their journey from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on observations of axon-BM interactions.

claim: Laminin BM-like accumulation cannot be detected in sly -/- mutants at all analyzed stages from 16 to 36 hpf.
source: As previously observed (Dolez et al., 2011; Parsons et al., 2002; Stemple et al., 1996; Wiellette et al., 2004), Laminin BM-like accumulation could not be detected in sly -/- mutants (referred to as sly mutants) at all the analysed stages, from 16 to 36 hpf, while heterozygous sly +/- embryos displayed an expression pattern that was similar to sly +/+ embryos (Figure 2A–C').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-C' and cited previous studies.

claim: Heterozygous sly +/- embryos display a Laminin expression pattern similar to sly +/+ embryos.
source: As previously observed (Dolez et al., 2011; Parsons et al., 2002; Stemple et al., 1996; Wiellette et al., 2004), Laminin BM-like accumulation could not be detected in sly -/- mutants (referred to as sly mutants) at all the analysed stages, from 16 to 36 hpf, while heterozygous sly +/- embryos displayed an expression pattern that was similar to sly +/+ embryos (Figure 2A–C').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-C'.

claim: There is likely no residual/maternal Laminin at the onset of OP coalescence in sly mutants.
source: This indicates that that there is likely no residual/maternal Laminin at the onset of OP coalescence.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Laminin detection from 16 hpf onwards.

claim: Nidogen is present in BM-like structures around the OP and the brain in control siblings at 22, 28 and 36 hpf.
source: Nidogen was present in BM-like structures around the OP and the brain in control siblings, with a pattern resembling that of Laminin, while in sly mutants no BM staining could be detected around the two tissues (Figure 2D–F').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D-F'.

claim: In sly mutants, no Nidogen BM staining can be detected around the OP and brain at 22, 28 and 36 hpf.
source: Nidogen was present in BM-like structures around the OP and the brain in control siblings, with a pattern resembling that of Laminin, while in sly mutants no BM staining could be detected around the two tissues (Figure 2D–F').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D-F'.

claim: In controls, Collagen IV is present in the linear BMs around the OP and the brain, and with a more fibrous distribution in the mesenchymal tissues surrounding the OP.
source: In controls, Collagen IV was present in the linear BMs around the OP and the brain, and, with a more fibrous distribution, in the mesenchymal tissues surrounding the OP.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: In sly mutants, Collagen IV immunoreactive pattern is dramatically disrupted but not totally abolished.
source: In sly mutants, Collagen IV immunoreactive pattern was dramatically disrupted, but not totally abolished: the BM-like linear staining was absent, but discrete patches of fibrous expression remained around the OP, at various locations (Figure 2G–I').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G-I'.

claim: In sly mutants, the BM-like linear Collagen IV staining is absent, but discrete patches of fibrous expression remain around the OP.
source: In sly mutants, Collagen IV immunoreactive pattern was dramatically disrupted, but not totally abolished: the BM-like linear staining was absent, but discrete patches of fibrous expression remained around the OP, at various locations (Figure 2G–I').
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G-I'.

claim: At 24 hpf in controls, the plasma membranes of NCC are separated from those of adjacent OP and brain cells by a 120 nm-wide gap containing electron dense ECM material.
source: At 24 hpf in controls, the plasma membranes of NCC were separated from those of adjacent OP and brain cells by a 120 nm-wide gap containing electron dense ECM material (Figure 2J and M).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2J and M.

claim: The electron dense ECM material between NCC and adjacent OP/brain cells in controls likely represents the BMs of the two tissues.
source: This material likely represents the BMs of the two tissues, with morphological features resembling those of BMs found in other tissues of zebrafish embryos at similar stages (Bryan et al., 2020; Yamaguchi et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from morphological features and cited previous studies.

claim: In sly mutants at 24 hpf, almost no NCC can be detected.
source: In sly mutants, almost no NCC could be detected, suggesting that NCC development is affected.
evidence: Inferred from electron microscopy observations.

claim: NCC development is affected in sly mutants.
source: In sly mutants, almost no NCC could be detected, suggesting that NCC development is affected.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of NCC in electron microscopy images.

claim: In sly mutants at 24 hpf, the plasma membranes of OP and brain cells are separated by a 40 nm-wide gap, which is significantly smaller than in controls.
source: In this mutant context, the plasma membranes of OP and brain cells were separated by a 40 nm-wide gap, which was significantly smaller than in controls.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2J, J' and M.

claim: In sly mutants at 24 hpf, the gap between OP and brain cells is most often devoid of electron dense material.
source: This gap was most often devoid of electron dense material (only rare spots could be detected, Figure 2J, J' and M).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2J, J' and M.

claim: A similar trend of reduced intercellular gap between OP and brain cells is detected at 32 hpf in sly mutants.
source: A similar trend was detected at 32 hpf (Figure 2K, K' and N).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2K, K' and N.

claim: The thickness of the intercellular gaps within the OP or the brain is not affected in sly mutants.
source: By contrast, the thickness of the intercellular gaps within the OP or the brain was not affected in mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The integrity of the OP and brain BMs is strongly affected in sly mutants.
source: The integrity of the OP and brain BMs is thus strongly affected in sly mutants, as previously reported in other tissues of Laminin γ1 mutants (Urbano et al., 2009; Yamada et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from electron microscopy observations and cited previous studies.

claim: The ML dimension of the Tg(neurog1:GFP)+ OP cell clusters is increased in sly mutants at 22 hpf.
source: While no difference was found for anteroposterior (AP) and dorsoventral (DV) dimensions, the mediolateral (ML) dimension was increased in mutants (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: No difference is found in the AP and DV dimensions of the Tg(neurog1:GFP)+ OP cell clusters between sly mutants and controls at 22 hpf.
source: While no difference was found for anteroposterior (AP) and dorsoventral (DV) dimensions, the mediolateral (ML) dimension was increased in mutants (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: No difference is found in the number of mitotic cells in the OPs of sly mutants and control siblings at 16 and 21 hpf.
source: This could be the consequence of an increased number of GFP+ cells; however, no difference was found in the number of mitotic cells in the OPs of sly mutants and control siblings at 16 and 21 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, E, F)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, E, F.

claim: Sly mutants exhibit a tendency for increased apoptosis in the OP.
source: and, as previously reported in other tissues (Parsons et al., 2002), we observed a tendency for the sly mutants to exhibit increased apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, J, M, N).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, J, M, N and cited previous study.

claim: No significant difference is observed for the MSD of OP cells between controls and sly mutants during OP coalescence.
source: No significant difference was observed for the MSD of OP cells between controls and sly mutants, but the MSD was higher for brain cells in the mutants (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The MSD is higher for brain cells in sly mutants compared to controls during OP coalescence.
source: No significant difference was observed for the MSD of OP cells between controls and sly mutants, but the MSD was higher for brain cells in the mutants (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: OP cells do not show any change in their total ML displacement during OP coalescence in sly mutants.
source: Direction wise, surprisingly OP cells did not show any change in their total ML displacement (Figure 3L), nor in their DV displacement (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: OP cells do not show any change in their DV displacement during OP coalescence in sly mutants.
source: Direction wise, surprisingly OP cells did not show any change in their total ML displacement (Figure 3L), nor in their DV displacement (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: In sly mutants, anterior OP cells tend to migrate less posteriorly during OP coalescence.
source: Differences, although not statistically significant, could be detected along the AP axis for anterior, central, and posterior OP cells: in the mutants the anterior cohort of cells tended to migrate less posteriorly, while central and posterior cells migrated more anteriorly, as if the final cell positions were all shifted towards more anterior locations (Figure 3N–P).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3N-P.

claim: In sly mutants, central and posterior OP cells migrate more anteriorly during OP coalescence.
source: Differences, although not statistically significant, could be detected along the AP axis for anterior, central, and posterior OP cells: in the mutants the anterior cohort of cells tended to migrate less posteriorly, while central and posterior cells migrated more anteriorly, as if the final cell positions were all shifted towards more anterior locations (Figure 3N–P).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3N-P.

claim: The position of the OP along the AP axis may be shifted anteriorly at the end of OP coalescence in sly mutants.
source: It is possible however that the position of the OP along the AP axis is shifted anteriorly at the end of OP coalescence.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the AP displacement data.

claim: Overall OP cell movements occur with normal parameters and allow the condensation of OPs into compact neuronal clusters in sly mutants.
source: In conclusion, while the movements of brain cells are increased in the absence of BMs at coalescence stages, overall the OP cell movements occur with normal parameters and allow the condensation of OPs into compact neuronal clusters in the sly mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of cell tracking data.

claim: A marked anterior and ventral departure of brain cells occurs in control embryos from 24 to 26 hpf, representing the onset of the flexure movement.
source: From 24 to 26 hpf we observed a marked anterior and ventral departure of brain cells in control embryos, representing the onset of the flexure movement.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: OP cells move anteriorly and ventrally from 24-26 hpf in coordination with the brain, revealing that the OPs are subjected to the flexure movement.
source: Strikingly, OP cells also moved anteriorly and ventrally from these stages, in coordination with the brain, revealing that the OPs are also subjected to the flexure movement (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: The flexure movements are visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants.
source: The flexure movements were also visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, Figure 4—video 1), with OP cells moving with a higher MSD than in controls (Figure 4M).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: OP cells in sly mutants move with a higher MSD than in controls during the forebrain flexure.
source: The flexure movements were also visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, Figure 4—video 1), with OP cells moving with a higher MSD than in controls (Figure 4M).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: A similar trend of higher MSD is observed for brain cells in sly mutants during the forebrain flexure, but is not statistically significant.
source: A similar trend was observed for brain cells, but was not statistically significant (Figure 4N).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: In 4/4 sly mutant embryos, brain and OP cells exhibit curved trajectories, moving first anteriorly and ventrally, then turning posteriorly.
source: Moreover, upon visualisation of the cell trajectories in a lateral (YZ) view, we noticed that in 4/4 mutant embryos, brain and OP cells exhibited curved trajectories, moving first anteriorly and ventrally, then turning posteriorly, while this phenomenon occurred in only 1/4 control sibling during the duration of our movies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N.

claim: Brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in sly mutants.
source: This reinforces the idea that brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in the sly mutants, and suggests that in the wild type situation the BMs allow the tissues, and in particular the OP, to resist to the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of curved trajectories and higher MSD in mutants.

claim: In the wild type situation, the BMs allow the tissues, particularly the OP, to resist the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
source: This reinforces the idea that brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in the sly mutants, and suggests that in the wild type situation the BMs allow the tissues, and in particular the OP, to resist to the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of cell behaviors in mutants and controls.

claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering during the forebrain flexure.
source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of ectopic cells and altered OP shape in mutants.

claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to maintain OP shape during the forebrain flexure.
source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased DV dimension in mutants.

claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of higher MSD in mutants.

claim: In control siblings, OP cells display a lateral displacement during the forebrain flexure.
source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J and O.

claim: In sly mutants, OP cells move in the medial direction towards the brain during the forebrain flexure.
source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4L and O.

claim: The two OPs progressively converge towards each other in sly mutants during the forebrain flexure.
source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of medial OP cell movement in mutants.

claim: OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue.
source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: OPs in sly mutants display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain.
source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: The frontier between the OP and brain appears as a straight line in control siblings.
source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: The width of the forebrain in sly mutants is smaller than in controls, particularly in anterior and dorsal areas.
source: The width of the forebrain in sly mutants was smaller than in controls, in particular in anterior and dorsal areas (Figure 5B-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Proliferation is unchanged in the brain of sly mutants.
source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L.

claim: Apoptosis is only slightly increased in the brain of sly mutants.
source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L.

claim: The smaller brain width in sly mutants is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that proliferation is unchanged and apoptosis is only slightly increased.

claim: The OP/brain boundary is less straight in sly mutants compared to controls at 36 hpf.
source: This analysis demonstrated that the OP/brain boundary is less straight in sly mutants as compared with controls (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The forebrain is smaller and distorted in sly mutants, possibly due to the inward convergence of the two OPs.
source: Thus, our analyses of cell tracks, brain size and proliferation/apoptosis, and of the shape of the brain/OP boundary suggest that the forebrain is smaller and distorted in sly mutants, possibly due to the inward convergence of the two OPs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including cell tracks, brain size, and boundary shape.

claim: The brain may fail to form in the normal size and shape in sly mutants.
source: A non-mutually alternative hypothesis is that the brain fails to form in the normal size and shape in sly mutants.
evidence: Speculative alternative hypothesis.

claim: The Laminin γ1-dependent BMs serve to establish a straight brain/OP boundary preventing local intermixing and late convergence of the two OPs.
source: These findings suggest that the Laminin γ1-dependent BMs serve to establish a straight brain/OP boundary preventing local intermixing and the late convergence of the two OPs towards each other during the flexure movement.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of irregular boundary and OP convergence in mutants.

claim: Retrograde axon extension appears not to be affected in sly mutants for at least some of the neurog1:GFP+ neurons/axons.
source: Several instances of retrograde extension were seen both in controls and mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating that retrograde axon extension occurs normally for at least some of the neurog1:GFP+ neurons/axons in sly mutants.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Retrograde axon extension occurs normally for at least some of the YFP+ OP neurons in sly mutants.
source: In addition, on fixed Tg(omp:meYFP) sly mutants at 24 hpf, numerous YFP+ neurons had their proximal axonal portion formed and attached to the brain surface (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that retrograde axon extension also occurs normally for at least some of the YFP+ OP neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: The presence of a BM around the OP and/or the brain is not an absolute requirement for the attachment of axon tips to the ventro-medial wall of the OP during retrograde extension.
source: Although we cannot rule out that retrograde axon extension is affected in a subset of OP neurons, for instance in ectopic cells, the presence of a BM around the OP and/or the brain appears not to be an absolute requirement for the attachment of axon tips to the ventro-medial wall of the OP during retrograde extension.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claim: In sly mutant embryos, most YFP+ axonal protrusions are unable to leave the OP and appear to stall at the OP/brain boundary.
source: In mutant embryos, severe axonal defects were observed. Most YFP+ axonal protrusions were unable to leave the OP and appeared to stall at the OP/brain boundary, leading in some embryos to an apparent absence of axon bundle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, left column and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 4—video 2.

claim: In some sly mutant embryos (8-10%), a small proportion of axons manage to form a bundle reaching the presumptive OB region by ectopically exiting the OP dorsally.
source: In some embryos (8–10%), a small proportion of axons managed form a bundle reaching the presumptive OB region by ectopically exiting the OP dorsally (an exit point location never observed in the control fish), while the axons would normally exit the OP at a more ventro-medial position in the controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, left column and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 4—video 2.

claim: An increased proportion of embryos with ectopic medial projections is observed in sly mutants (18-30% depending on the stage, compared to 0-9% in controls).
source: In addition, an increased proportion of embryos with ectopic medial projections was observed in mutants (18–30% of the embryos depending on the stage, as compared to 0 to 9% in controls, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, right column).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: There is a tendency for a higher percentage of embryos displaying ventral projections in sly mutants, particularly visible at 24 hpf.
source: Finally, there is a tendency for a higher percentage of embryos displaying ventral projections in the sly mutant, particularly visible at 24 hpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, middle column).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Growth cones in sly mutants do not display a directional migration towards the bulb during the whole movie duration.
source: By contrast, growth cones in the sly mutants did not display a directional migration towards the bulb, during the whole movie duration (Figure 6C, F1 and L).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6C, F1 and L.

claim: Growth cones in sly mutants are motile and explore the environment, but move on short distances and/or without preferential direction, resulting in perturbed axon growth.
source: They were motile and explored the environment, as shown by speed and persistence measurements, but moved on short distances and/or without preferential direction, resulting in a perturbed axon growth (Figure 6C–N).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C-N.

claim: The migration of the olfactory axons is impaired in sly mutants.
source: These live imaging analyses confirm that the migration of the olfactory axons is impaired in sly mutants.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of growth cone behavior.

claim: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for the growth and navigation of the axons from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
source: Altogether, our results show that Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for the growth and navigation of the axons from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of severe axonal defects in mutants.

claim: Crestin-labelled NCC are absent from the brain/OP interface in sly mutants at 32 hpf.
source: In situ hybridisation for the NCC marker crestin (Luo et al., 2001) revealed that, while a clear NCC cluster can be seen at the brain/OP interface in controls at 32 hpf, crestin-labelled NCC are absent from this area in sly mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, A').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, A'.

claim: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are important for NCC migration or survival in the brain/OP interface region.
source: This suggests that Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are important for NCC migration or survival in this region of the embryo.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of NCC at the brain/OP interface in mutants.

claim: In sly mutants, numerous motile NCC are observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all analyzed placodes (8/8).
source: Surprisingly, in sly mutants, numerous motile NCC were also observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all the analysed placodes (8/8), and populated the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes (10/10 in controls; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In sly mutants, NCC populate the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes.
source: Surprisingly, in sly mutants, numerous motile NCC were also observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all the analysed placodes (8/8), and populated the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes (10/10 in controls; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In sly mutants, NCC are observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes.
source: By contrast, in sly mutants, NCC were observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes, and in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes as well.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In sly mutants, NCC are observed in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes.
source: By contrast, in sly mutants, NCC were observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes, and in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes as well.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In sly mutants, NCC that initially populated the ventral brain/OP interface are expelled from the boundary at later stages.
source: Interestingly, in these two samples, NCC that had initially populated the ventral brain/OP interface were then expelled from the boundary at later stages (Figure 5—video 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—video 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The migration of cranial NCC towards the OP and between the eye and OP is only partially impaired in sly mutants.
source: Altogether, these live imaging data suggest that the migration of cranial NCC towards the OP and between the eye and OP is only partially impaired in sly mutants.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of NCC migration.

claim: The subset of NCC that populate the OP/forebrain appears to be more specifically affected in sly mutants, with defects in their migration to the interface and/or the maintenance of their position at the interface.
source: The subset of NCC that populate the OP/forebrain appears to be more specifically affected, with defects in their migration to the interface and/or the maintenance of their position at the interface.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of NCC behavior at the OP/forebrain interface.

claim: No significant difference is observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for OP dimensions and axon bundle length at 28 and 36 hpf.
source: No significant difference was observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for these parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–L), suggesting that the late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-L.

claim: The late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
source: No significant difference was observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for these parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–L), suggesting that the late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of sly and foxd3 mutant phenotypes.

claim: The BM of the OP prevents its deformation in response to the mechanical forces generated by the morphogenetic movement of the neighbouring brain.
source: We thus propose that the BM of the OP prevents its deformation in response to the mechanical forces generated by the morphogenetic movement of the neighbouring brain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the OP deforms in mutants lacking BMs during the flexure.

claim: The ability of the placode's BM to limit the deformation of the OP during the flexure most probably relies on its stiffness.
source: The ability of the placode's BM to limit the deformation of the OP during this developmental step most probably relies on its stiffness.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known mechanical properties of BMs.

claim: In the Drosophila egg chamber, Collagen IV has a major contribution to BM mechanical properties, particularly to its stiffness.
source: In the Drosophila egg chamber, while Laminin itself has a minor contribution to the BM mechanical properties, Collagen IV, which deposition in the BM depends on Laminin (Díaz de la Loza et al., 2017) has a major contribution to these properties, and in particular to its stiffness (Töpfer et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The putative loss of mechanical properties leading to OP deformation in the sly mutant may be due to Collagen IV rather than Laminin itself.
source: Even though the putative loss of mechanical properties leading to OP deformation observed in the sly mutant is a consequence of a Laminin loss-of-function, it remains conceivable that it is the Collagen IV, rather than the Laminin itself, which is responsible of these mechanical properties in wild-type animals.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the role of Collagen IV in other systems.

claim: A dramatic consequence of the absence of proper OP and brain BMs in the sly mutant is the irregular and undefined frontier between the brain and OP.
source: A dramatic consequence of the absence of proper OP and brain BMs in the sly mutant is the irregular and undefined frontier between the brain and OP, with placodal cells tending to locally intermingle with brain cells, and vice versa, along the OP/brain interface.
evidence: Inferred from observations of the brain/OP boundary in mutants.

claim: Tissue intermixing has been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans.
source: Tissue intermixing has also been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans (Huang et al., 2003) and in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of the Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor (Buisson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tissue intermixing has been observed in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor.
source: Tissue intermixing has also been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans (Huang et al., 2003) and in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of the Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor (Buisson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The absence of a clear boundary between the OP and the brain in the sly mutant is accompanied by an apparent distortion of the brain, with notably reduced dimension in its medio-lateral axis.
source: The absence of a clear boundary between the OP and the brain in the sly mutant is accompanied by an apparent distortion of the brain, with notable reduced dimension in its medio-lateral axis.
evidence: Inferred from measurements of brain width in mutants.

claim: The brain distortion in sly mutants is possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain.
source: This phenotype, possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain, illustrates an additional and unexpected role of the OP and brain BMs, in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the brain distortion phenotype.

claim: The OP and brain BMs play a role in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
source: This phenotype, possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain, illustrates an additional and unexpected role of the OP and brain BMs, in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of OP convergence in mutants.

claim: The early development of zebrafish olfactory axons begins with their retrograde extension, involving the attachment of the tips of the axonal protrusions to the brain's surface, followed by a lateral movement of the OP cell bodies in the opposite direction.
source: The early development of zebrafish olfactory axons begins with their retrograde extension, involving the attachment of the tips of the axonal protrusions to the brain's surface, followed by a lateral movement of the OP cell bodies in the opposite direction (Breau et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for retrograde axon extension in the olfactory system.
source: These results suggest that Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for this retrograde axon extension and, more specifically, that Laminin γ1 itself or other components of the BMs are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of those axon tips onto the brain's surface, which is a prerequisite for their retrograde extension.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claim: Laminin γ1 or other BM components are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of axon tips onto the brain's surface during retrograde extension.
source: These results suggest that Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for this retrograde axon extension and, more specifically, that Laminin γ1 itself or other components of the BMs are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of those axon tips onto the brain's surface, which is a prerequisite for their retrograde extension.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claim: Following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones.
source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claim: The olfactory axons assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP.
source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claim: The olfactory axons turn and migrate dorsally for a short distance between both BMs.
source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claim: The olfactory axons cross the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claim: The olfactory axons have to cross two BMs during their development.
source: In other words, the olfactory axons have to cross two BMs.
evidence: Inferred from the description of axon behavior.

claim: The axons cross the first BM as it is still under construction and contains perforations, taking advantage of BM-free small pores to exit the OP.
source: Our data show that the axons cross the first BM as it is still under construction and contains perforations, thus taking advantage of BM-free small pores to exit the OP and reach the narrow area located between the two BMs.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of BM assembly and axon exit.

claim: The axons may locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases to enter the brain.
source: It will be interesting, in future work, to determine whether the axons locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases, or displace the BM with protrusive forces, or use a combination of both mechanisms (Chang and Chaudhuri, 2019; Ihara et al., 2011; Nazari et al., 2022; Yamada et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation, supported by citations.

claim: The axons may displace the BM with protrusive forces to enter the brain.
source: It will be interesting, in future work, to determine whether the axons locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases, or displace the BM with protrusive forces, or use a combination of both mechanisms (Chang and Chaudhuri, 2019; Ihara et al., 2011; Nazari et al., 2022; Yamada et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation, supported by citations.

claim: Olfactory axons remain confined in close proximity to the Laminin-rich BMs as they migrate in the narrow corridor between the OP and brain BMs.
source: As they migrate in the narrow corridor between the OP and brain BMs, olfactory axons remain confined in close proximity to the Laminin-rich BMs.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations.

claim: Once in the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of the olfactory axon bundle grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM.
source: Importantly, once they have reached the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of this axon bundle still grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting that this BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of these axons.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations.

claim: The brain's BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of olfactory axons.
source: Importantly, once they have reached the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of this axon bundle still grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting that this BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of these axons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that axon tips grow along the BM.

claim: The axon growth and directionality phenotype in sly mutants is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation.
source: This phenotype is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation, as demonstrated by HuC immunolabelling and expression of the Tg(neurog1:GFP) and Tg(omp:meYFP) transgenes, which do not show obvious difference as compared to control animals, but appears to be rather due to axon growth and navigation defects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neuronal markers are expressed normally in mutants.

claim: The axon phenotype in sly mutants appears to be due to axon growth and navigation defects.
source: This phenotype is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation, as demonstrated by HuC immunolabelling and expression of the Tg(neurog1:GFP) and Tg(omp:meYFP) transgenes, which do not show obvious difference as compared to control animals, but appears to be rather due to axon growth and navigation defects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of impaired axon migration in mutants.

claim: Laminin is a good candidate for acting as a privileged substrate for olfactory axons.
source: We did not formally identify the component(s) of the BM involved in this axon extension and pathfinding, but we consider Laminin itself as a good candidate for acting as a privileged substrate the axons, as Laminin does so for other populations of axons in zebrafish (Paulus and Halloran, 2006; Semina et al., 2006), and has been shown in rodents to favor OSN axon extension in vitro, and to be present in vivo along the path followed by OSN axons from the olfactory epithelium to the bulb (Kafitz and Greer, 1997).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Laminin accelerates the growth of axons through binding to integrins, which favors the formation of F-actin in the growth cone in a microtubule- and Rac1-dependent manner.
source: From a molecular point of view, it has been established on cultured sympathetic neurons that Laminin accelerates the growth of axons through binding to integrins, which favors the formation of F-actin in the growth cone in a microtubule- and Rac1-dependent manner (Grabham et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Laminin promotes hippocampal neuron growth cone enhanced progression on stiff substrate through its interaction with L1, highlighting a mechanosensitive axon outgrowth mediated by a L1-Laminin clutch mechanism.
source: Recently, Abe et al., 2021 further documented another role of Laminin in promoting hippocampal neuron growth cones enhanced progression on stiff substrate, through its interaction with L1, highlighting a new mechanosensitive axon outgrowth mediated by a L1-Laminin clutch mechanism (Abe et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Other components of the BM, also affected in the sly mutant, may be involved in the regulation of olfactory axon development.
source: Other components of the BM, also affected in the sly mutant, may be involved as well in the regulation of olfactory axon development.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis.

claim: In rodents, the characterization of ECM protein expression along the developing olfactory pathway revealed a complex interplay between ECM permissive and inhibitory cues expressed dynamically, appearing to restrict axons to the pathway while promoting axon outgrowth within.
source: Still in rodents indeed, the characterisation of the expression of ECM proteins along the developing olfactory pathway unraveled a complex interplay between ECM permissive and inhibitory cues expressed in a dynamic way, appearing to restrict axons to the pathway while promoting axon outgrowth within (Shay et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Guidance cues interacting with BM molecules may be involved in some aspects of the axonal defects observed in the sly mutant.
source: In addition to ECM molecules present in the BMs, guidance cues interacting with these molecules may also be involved in some aspects of the axonal defects observed in the sly mutant.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis.

claim: Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin but attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin.
source: For example, while Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin, they are attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin (Weinl et al., 2003), and Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of these axons to repulsion (Höpker et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of Xenopus retinal axons to repulsion.
source: For example, while Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin, they are attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin (Weinl et al., 2003), and Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of these axons to repulsion (Höpker et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The repulsive effect of slit2 on Robo expressing axons of dorsal root ganglia neurons is lost in absence of Laminin.
source: Moreover, whereas slit2 repulses Robo expressing axons of dorsal root ganglia neurons, this repulsive effect is lost in absence of Laminin (Nguyen-Ba-Charvet et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Netrin1a and 1b are expressed in the zebrafish forebrain close to the route of the olfactory axons, where they play an attractive role for olfactory axons which express the netrin receptor DCC.
source: Netrin1a and 1b are expressed in the zebrafish forebrain close to the route of the axons, where they play an attractive role for olfactory axons which express the netrin receptor DCC (Dang et al., 2023; Lakhina et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several ephrin and slits ligands are expressed in the forebrain at stages of axonal growth.
source: In addition, several ephrin and slits ligands are expressed in the forebrain at stages of axonal growth (https://zfin.org/, Miyasaka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to database and previous literature.

claim: The absence of Laminin in the sly mutant may change the netrin-, ephrin- or slit-dependent pathfinding of olfactory axons.
source: We may thus envisage that the absence of Laminin in the sly mutant may change in some way the netrin-, ephrin- or slit-dependent pathfinding of olfactory axons.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on known interactions between Laminin and guidance cues.

claim: The boundary between the sensory and central components of the olfactory system is organised by the BMs of the OP and the brain.
source: In conclusion, our findings indicate that the boundary between the sensory and central components of the olfactory system (Suter and Jaworski, 2019) is organised by the BMs of the OP and the brain.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of BM function in organizing the OP/brain boundary.

claim: The BMs of the OP and brain are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb.
source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
evidence: Inferred from observations of BM interruptions at exit/entry points and axon-BM interactions.

claim: The BMs of the OP and brain maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occurring during the brain flexure.
source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
evidence: Inferred from observations of OP deformation and displacement in mutants lacking BMs.

claim: The BMs of the OP and brain ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
evidence: Inferred from observations of tissue intermixing in mutants lacking BMs.
